# Fairchild and the Platform Company {#sec-4-03}

::: {.chapter-meta}
Act III — The Silicon Valley Machine · 1957–1968
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="draft"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Pre-Draft Brief

**Core question.** How does one firm seed an entire industry?

**The answer.** By fragmenting productively. Fairchild's importance is not that
it dominated but that it decomposed: Intel, AMD, National Semiconductor and
dozens of others came out of it, each carrying the same techniques and the same
assumptions. And in financing that decomposition, Arthur Rock invented the
modern venture model — equity rather than lending, people rather than assets.

**The mechanism.** Chokepoint control, distributed, plus the birth of the
capital chokepoint that ch. 5 will formalise. The planar process is a genuine
bottleneck; what makes the Valley rather than merely a company is that the
bottleneck's holders kept splitting and each split was funded.

**The key fact.** Robert Noyce's independent development of the integrated
circuit, and Jean Hoerni's planar process, gave Fairchild a manufacturing
advantage that could be carried out of the building in people's heads. The asset
was fully portable, which is exactly why the firm could not hold it.

**The human anchor.** Arthur Rock, the least visible figure in the story,
deciding that the thing worth buying is a group of people rather than a factory.

**Excluded voices.** The assembly and fabrication workforce, disproportionately
women and, as the decade progresses, offshore. Fairchild's Hong Kong assembly
operation opened in 1963 — the offshore turn happening in semiconductors at the
same moment Knight is arranging it in shoes, two chapters later. Make the
connection.

**Proof.** This chapter proves that recombination rather than accumulation drove
the Valley by showing that its dominant firms are all descendants of a single
company that lost its people.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Working summary

Draw the family tree of the American semiconductor industry and almost every
branch runs back to one company that could not keep its people. Intel, AMD,
National Semiconductor, and dozens more came out of Fairchild, and the chapter
begins with that fan-out and then explains why the parent could not prevent it.

Fairchild Semiconductor was founded in 1957 by the eight who had left Shockley,
under a deal with Fairchild Camera and Instrument that included a buyback option
which later caused most of the trouble. Its technical achievements were real and
consequential: Jean Hoerni's planar process, and Robert Noyce's independent
development of the integrated circuit. Together they gave the firm a
manufacturing advantage over everyone else in the industry.

That advantage was also completely portable, which is the chapter's structural
point. Process knowledge lives in the people who hold it, and people can walk. A
company whose competitive position consists of things its engineers know cannot
prevent those engineers from founding competitors, particularly in a state that
will not enforce a non-compete. Noyce and Gordon Moore left for Intel in 1968;
Jerry Sanders founded AMD; Charlie Sporck went to National. The Valley grew by
recombination, splitting and re-forming faster than any regulator could follow.

The early customers were military and aerospace, including Minuteman and Apollo.
This is not yet a consumer industry, and the chapter keeps Act II's substrate
visible.

Arthur Rock's contribution runs alongside. He took equity rather than issuing
loans, and backed groups of people rather than collateral, which was genuinely
novel and which is what made funding the fragmentation possible.

Fairchild opened assembly operations in Hong Kong in 1963. That is the offshore
turn happening in semiconductors at the same moment Phil Knight is arranging it
in footwear three chapters later, and the workforce — largely young women, paid
a fraction of American wages — is the cost the margins depend on. Women on the
domestic fabrication lines belong in the same accounting.
:::

::: {.chapter-question}
How does one firm seed an entire industry?
:::

Draw the family tree of the American semiconductor industry and it is almost
entirely descended from one company that could not keep its people.

Intel. Advanced Micro Devices. National Semiconductor. Signetics. Intersil.
Teledyne's semiconductor operations. By the mid-1980s the number of firms
founded by Fairchild alumni or by their alumni in turn ran into the dozens, and
they were called Fairchildren, which is a joke that describes a mechanism.

## What Fairchild had

The technical achievements were real and they were fundamental.

Jean Hoerni developed the planar process, in which the transistor is built in
layers on a flat silicon surface protected by an oxide coating. Before it,
transistors were three-dimensional objects assembled individually and vulnerable
to contamination. After it, they could be fabricated photographically in
batches, reliably, at scale.

Robert Noyce then saw what followed. If devices could be built on a flat
surface, several of them could be built on the same piece of silicon and
connected with metal deposited on the same surface. Jack Kilby at Texas
Instruments had independently built an integrated circuit some months earlier by
a different method; Noyce's planar version was the one that could be
manufactured. The two companies litigated for years and eventually cross-
licensed.

That combination gave Fairchild a manufacturing advantage that no competitor
could match for several years.

## Why the advantage walked

The advantage was also completely portable, and this is the chapter's structural
point.

Process knowledge in semiconductor manufacturing lives in people. It is not
principally in patents, which describe the general approach and not the thousand
adjustments that make a line yield; and it is not in equipment, which anyone can
buy. It is in the engineers who know what temperature, what timing, what
contaminant caused last month's failures.

A company whose competitive position consists of what its engineers know cannot
prevent those engineers from leaving, particularly in a state that will not
enforce a non-compete. And Fairchild's parent company managed to give them
reasons.

Fairchild Camera and Instrument had exercised its option and bought the
subsidiary in 1959, which made the eight founders wealthy and made them
employees. The parent then treated the semiconductor division as a source of
cash for the rest of its business, declined to grant meaningful stock options to
the people generating the profits, and appointed executives from outside.

The departures began early — Hoerni, Last, and Roberts left in 1961 to found
Amelco under Teledyne — and accelerated. Charlie Sporck went to National
Semiconductor in 1967. Jerry Sanders left and founded AMD in 1969. And in 1968
Noyce and Gordon Moore resigned to found Intel, taking Andy Grove with them, and
Arthur Rock raised the money in a matter of days.

## Recombination as growth

What this produced is an industry that grew by splitting rather than by
accumulating, and the chapter should be precise about why that is unusual.

The normal pattern in a capital-intensive industry with strong learning effects
is consolidation. Advantages compound, the leader gets further ahead, and the
market ends up with a few large firms. That is what happened in steel, in
automobiles, and in aircraft.

Semiconductors went the other way for twenty years, because the crucial asset
kept walking out and because there was now a financial mechanism to fund it when
it did. Each new firm carried the same techniques and the same assumptions about
how a semiconductor company should be run — flat, engineering-led, generous with
equity — and each seeded the next.

The region acquired an industry rather than a company, and an industry with a
shared culture that had propagated by fission from a single origin.

## The military customer

The chapter keeps Act II's substrate visible, because the early market was not
consumer electronics and was not close to it.

Integrated circuits were expensive and their first large customers were
programmes for which cost mattered less than weight and reliability: the
Minuteman missile guidance system and the Apollo Guidance Computer. Federal
purchasing in the early 1960s absorbed the great majority of American integrated
circuit production and, by guaranteeing volume, drove the price down the
learning curve to the point where commercial applications became viable.

The consumer semiconductor industry exists because the Defense Department and
NASA bought the first several years of output at whatever it cost. That is a
public subsidy of the most direct kind, and it does not appear in any account of
the industry that begins with a garage.

## Moore's observation

In 1965 Gordon Moore, then Fairchild's director of research and development, was
asked by *Electronics* magazine to write about the future of integrated
electronics. He plotted the number of components on a chip against time, found
the count had been doubling roughly annually, and projected the trend forward a
decade.

It held, with a revision to roughly two years, for half a century.

Moore's law is usually described as a prediction and it is better understood as
a coordination device. It was not a law of physics. It was a statement about
what the industry could achieve if it kept investing at a particular rate, and
once everyone believed it, everyone planned around it — equipment suppliers,
chip designers, and the customers designing products for chips that did not yet
exist. A shared expectation about the future became a schedule, and firms that
missed it lost their market.

The chapter's interest is that this is an industry setting its own clock. The
rate of technical progress in semiconductors between 1965 and roughly 2015 was
determined substantially by a self-fulfilling forecast published in a trade
magazine by a research director who would found Intel three years later.

It also has a chokepoint consequence, which arrives in Act III. Sustaining the
curve required exponentially rising capital investment in fabrication, and the
number of firms able to afford a leading-edge plant fell from dozens to a
handful. The economics that made the industry fragment in 1968 reversed
completely, and by the twenty-first century advanced fabrication had
concentrated into fewer facilities than any other critical technology on earth.

## Hong Kong, 1963

Fairchild opened an assembly plant in Hong Kong in 1963, and it is the first
entry in this act's ledger.

The logic was straightforward. Fabricating the wafer required capital and
expertise and stayed in California. Assembling and testing the resulting devices
— bonding fine wires, sealing packages, checking output — was labour-intensive,
required no advanced training, and could be done anywhere labour was cheap. Hong
Kong wages were a small fraction of Californian ones.

The workforce was overwhelmingly young women. So was the fabrication workforce
back in California, where women worked the lines in clean rooms handling
solvents and acids whose long-term effects were poorly understood at the time
and became the subject of litigation and epidemiological study decades later.
Semiconductor manufacturing in Santa Clara County also left a legacy of
groundwater contamination from solvent handling that produced one of the densest
concentrations of federal Superfund sites in the country, in the same towns
whose housing prices this book has already discussed.

Other firms followed to Hong Kong, then to South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore, and
Malaysia. The offshore assembly model was established in semiconductors by the
mid-1960s.

Note the date against the next chapter but one. In 1962 a Stanford business
student wrote a paper arguing that Japanese manufacturing could displace German
shoes, and by the end of the decade he was importing from Asian contract
factories. Fairchild reached the same conclusion in the same years, in silicon.
Neither was copying the other. Both were responding to the same arithmetic.

## What leaves the chapter

An industry that reproduces by fission. A technical asset that lives in people
and therefore cannot be held. A federal customer buying the early output. An
offshore labour system supplying the margin. And a financier who has worked out
how to fund a group of engineers walking out of a building.

That last one is about to become the tightest chokepoint in the system.
